## Learning Objectives

This lesson focuses on learning more about the different types of
geographic data and learning how to import and work with your own data
in ArcGIS Online. At the end of this workshop you will:

-   Have a better understanding of various vector and raster geospatial
    data types
-   Know how to import external tabular data into ArcGIS Online
-   Know how to edit or add data to a feature layer
-   Better understand the difference between continuous and categorical
    raster layers
-   Know how to export data from ArcGIS Online to your local machine

## Review: Annotations vs. Data

In [Workshop
1](https://rds.library.ucsb.edu/from-maps-to-analysis/01_make_map.html),
we started with sketch layers to draw points, lines, and polygons
directly on top of the map. While sketches are convenient for quick
markups and annotations, they are not true GIS data layers. Sketches
lack an underlying database table and cannot be queried, filtered, or
used in spatial analysis.

In contrast, **feature layers** link geometries (points, lines, or
polygons) to structured records in an **attribute table**. Each feature
has defined attributes, or fields (e.g., name, speed limit, road type,
elevation) with specific data types (such as text strings, numbers, and
dates). This tabular structure makes it possible to filter features,
symbolize data based on its attributes, and calculate spatial
relationships.

## Raster vs Vector Data

Geographic data generally falls into two primary models: **vector** and
**raster**.

![The difference in geospatial work is the same as between Adobe
Illustrator (vectors) and Photoshop (rasters) (image credit: [Graphic
Mama](https://graphicmama.com/blog/vector-and-raster-whats-the-difference/)](images/workshop2/graphicmamacartoon.jpg){fig-alt="A cartoon visually comparing mathematically calculated vectors veersus grids of square pixel rasters"}

### Vector Data

So far we have only looked at vector data. Vector data represents
discrete geographic features using coordinate geometry:

-   **Points**: Single $(X, Y)$ coordinate pairs representing discrete
    locations (e.g., bike racks, bus stops, accident locations).
-   **Lines (Polylines)**: Ordered sequences of vertices connecting
    locations to represent linear features or networks (e.g., bike
    paths, roads, transit routes, streams).
-   **Polygons**: Closed shapes enclosing an area defined by connected
    coordinate vertices (e.g., campus buildings, land parcels, parks,
    water bodies).

Every shape is tied to a row in an attribute table, where each column
holds specific properties describing that feature. For example, in our
Workshop 1 example, we can pop open the attribute table and look at the
attributes (the row) for the "Library" building:

Visually selecting the library building polygon on the map will select
the row in the attribute table.![Opening the Attribute
Table](images/workshop2/library-poly.png)

Then opening the Attribute Table under layer options by clicking Layers
\> UCSB Campus Buldings 2026, the `...` \> Show table![Library polygon
attributes](images/workshop2/library-attributes.png)

Each polygon in the table has many fields and values associated with it.
Building names, floor counts, area, who edited the file, and when it was
last updated, among other fields a user may find helpful when analyzing
their data.

Attributes may be divided into three types:

-   Nominal: free-text information for labels and names

-   Categorical

-   Numeric: both continuous and ordinal information that can be counted
    or has numerical importance - *ie* the number of floors that each
    building has (note: the UCSB Library has a basement and attic.
    Hence 10) or the area of each building's floorspace.

-   Continuous Numeric: information that can be ordered or ranked in
    some way - floor count

### Raster Data

Raster data represents the landscape as a regular grid of square cells
(pixels) organized into rows and columns.

-   **Single-band rasters**: Each pixel contains a single numerical
    value representing a continuous measurement (such as elevation in a
    Digital Elevation Model \[DEM\], slope, or temperature) or an
    integer code representing a category (such as land cover types).
-   **Multi-band rasters**: Each pixel contains multiple values across
    different spectral channels or bands (such as red, green, blue, and
    near-infrared bands in aerial photography or satellite imagery).

Below is a single band raster. The value of each pixel is elevation.
**INCORRECT – this is the slope map**

![](images/workshop2/wkshp_2_dem_example.png)

Below is an 8-band raster with band #7 (near IR) as red, band #3 (green)
as green, and band #1 (coastal blue) as blue. This type of image
displays are often called "false-color" because they do not respect the
RGB channel alignment. This can help to highlight some features, such as
vegetation that has a strong signal in near infrared (NIR) wavelengths

![](images/workshop2/false_color.png)

### The Story So Far

In the first workshop, we created a bicycle map of campus and Isla Vista
using pre-existing data.

Our goal for part 2 is to plan a challenging and comfortable bicycle
route that leads from the UCSB campus into the surrounding Goleta
community and the Santa Ynez foothills. Ideally, we want to lock up near
a trailhead, and then put our bike on the bus on the way back to campus.

To accomplish this, we need to expand beyond campus bike paths and
incorporate regional road networks; we want to look at elevation data to
look for steep climbs and long views; and we need to find those bus
stops.

## Exploring Raster Data

When outside of ArcGIS Online, geospatial raster data comes in many
different formats. TIFFs, Grids, netCDF, iiif, web map services. Too
many to list!

-   ArcGIS Online variations: while many of these start somewhere as
    TIFFs, they are all ingested into AGO as flavors of
    `Tiled imagery layers`

Let's add a Digital Elevation Model to out map: `ucsb_local_dem`. By
default, a `single channel` or `one band` raster is displayed as
grayscale, with low values black and high values white.

Your map with DEM should look something like this by default:

![Digital Elevation Model added to the
map](images/workshop2/wkshp2_map_2_defaultDEM.png){fig-alt="By default, DEMs appear as almost black for low elevations to white for high elevations"
width="90%" fig-align="center"}

Each pixel, or cell, in our DEM represents bare-earth surface elevation
relative to a vertical datum (mean sea level). The `ucsb_local_dem`
dataset was derived from a high-resolution USGS LiDAR survey (3D
Elevation Program (3DEP)).

**POP QUIZ:** What do you think are the units of `ucsb_local_dem`?

A DEM is an example of a **continuous raster** as the values stored in
each cell correspond to a quantity gradient (elevation in meters)
changing in space . Other examples of continuous raster would be
precipitation measurements, air quality index, ocean salinity, or
distance from a road.

In the layer properties, explore the raster statistics: note the minimum
elevation near sea level (0) along the coast and slough, rising to
hundreds of feet in the foothills, as well as the grid cell resolution.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}

#### Applying a Continuous Divergent Color Scheme

Data that moves around a zero point, such as our batho-topo elevation
model, is knows as \*\* divergent \*\*. It is very helpful to your map
viewers to visualize this typ of data with a divergent color scheme.

By default, continuous raster layers display using a grayscale "Stretch"
renderer (low values '0' dark, and high values 255 light). To clearly
distinguish elevation changes across the coastal plain and mountains,
let's change the symbology to a continuous, diverging color ramp (e.g.,
a below-and-above zero diverging ramp or an elevation palette). Select
the DEM layer and open the Styles menu
(![](images/workshop2/styles_icon.png))

to use 'Stretch', we have to force zero to be the middle value. When we
need to do this, we look at the DEM's actual minimum and maximum values,
and take whichever number has the larger absolute value. Use that exact
number as both a negative minimum and a positive maximum in the
Statistics table. (e.g.: 1218 feet)

![](images/workshop2/dem_options.png)

Here is below an example of a widely used color scale for DEM, with
lower elevation display in blue and green and higher elevation in brown
and white.

![Digital Elevation Model with color
scale](images/workshop2/w2_dem_colored.png){fig-alt="Digital Elevation
Model with color scaled for DEM: white a higher elevation, blue and
green for lower elevation"
scale\](images/workshop2/w2_dem_colored.png){fig-alt="Digital Elevation
Model with color scaled for DEM: white a higer elevation, blue and green
for lower elevation" width="90%" fig-align="center"}

### Categorical Rasters - Land Cover

**Categorical vs. Continuous Data**

Continuous data are best represented by numbers, and are logically
consistent when you do so. Smaller numbers = less of some measurement.

On the other hand, categorical data can be text or numeric. The value of
any numbers used do not necessarily reflect any mathematical value, but
it may. For example, while the values below have a natural order (The 3
Little Piggies Construction Scale), the numbers are *ordinal* but
arbitrary:

-   1 = reinforced concrete or steel beam
-   2 = wood stick construction
-   3 = baked brick masonry
-   4 = adobe
-   5 = sun brick / mud daub
-   6 = straw bail

While elevation is a **continuous raster** (values change smoothly along
a numerical gradient representing a quantity), other rasters are
**categorical rasters** (e.g., land cover classification datasets from
the Living Atlas, where integer cell values represent categories such as
urban development, forest, or water).

![](images/workshop2/landcover_result.png)

Show the legend to see the category names. Open the attribute table to
compare it to what appears for vector data:

### Multi-band Rasters

So far we have worked with single-channel, or 1-band rasters. However,
perhaps we are more familiar with 3-channel images, because our eyes see
best in the red-green-blue color space. For geospatial data, think of
this as satellite or aerial views.

For digital images, 3 'bands' of wavelengths are stored separately. When
the computer combines them together, we humans see something akin to
what we see when we look at nature with our eyes. However, we can swap
in other bandwidths of radiation, such as near infrared, or microwave,
and see completely other things.

The DREAM Lab hosts several satellite views of campus created by Planet
Labs, a private satellite firm. Its fleet of PlanetScope satellites
captures imagery in 8 bandwidth divisions of the electromagnetic
spectrum. 8-band images. Let's add one of those layers now:

**placeholder for Planet image of Goleta**

## Layer Management, Rasters, and Additional Vectors

1.  **Re-order layers**: Ensure vector layers (roads and paths) remain
    on top of the raster elevation layers in the layer stack so they are
    not hidden.

2.  **Imagery Layers vs. Basemaps**:

    -   An **basemap** sits at the bottom of the map canvas, serving
        purely as a static background context. Esri has options that are
        satellite and aerial views.
    -   An **imagery layer** is a data layer added to your map stack. It
        can be re-ordered above or below other layers, adjusted with
        transparency and blend modes, queried for pixel values, and
        analyze for groundcover characteristics.

1.  **Re-order layers**: Ensure vector layers (roads and paths) remain
    on top of the raster elevation layers in the layer stack so they are

2.  **Imagery Layers vs Basemaps**:
    -   A **basemap** sits at the bottom of the map canvas, serving

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="CRS"}
### A note on Coordinate Reference Systems

In ArcGIS Online, the default projection and Coordinate Reference System
(CRS) is WGS 1984 Web Mercator Auxiliary Sphere (also referred as
[EPSG:3857](https://epsg.io/3857))

Coordinate systems can be divided into two main categories: Projected
and Geographic Coordinate Systems.

-   **Projected** Coordinate Systems use a 2D flat surface to define
    locations and is measured in linear units. Locations are identified
    by x,y coordinates

-   **Geographic** Coordinate Systems use a 3D spherical surface
    measured in angular units to define locations on earth. A point is
    referred by its latitude and longitude.

There are plethora of CRSs that all have different accuracy and other
advantages depending on your location and extent of your area of
interest. Here is a good website to look at the different CRSs:
<https://epsg.io/>
:::

**POP QUIZ:** Examine the csv file - does it tell you anything about the
coordinate system that we are dealing with?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}

## Editing Vector Data

Now that we have imported data into ArcGIS Online, we might also want to
modify this data. For vector data, we can modify the AGO Feature Layer
attributes and values stored in the underlying table or the feature
itself by editing locations and shapes, or adding and removing specific
features. For raster data, those transformations are generally done
using some form of calculation on the entire raster, or specific values
targeted via conditions, rather than by manually editing pixel values.
We will talk more about raster calculations in our third workshop. For
today, we will focus on editing vector data (or feature layers in ArcGIS
jargon) in this workshop.

::: {.callout-warning collapse="false"}
## This goes beyond the map

It is important to understand that when we are editing a feature layer,
it is independent of the map. You are actually changing the data stored
under your content.

This also means that you might not have the right to edit some of the
data you are using in your map because you do not own them! A potential
workaround is to create a local copy of the data, but some data provider
do not allow this either.
:::

### Editing Features

We noticed that some locations of trailhead on the Goleta Beach Park,
east of campus, are in the ocean. This is probably due to some

The top part (in red) of this panel lets you edit the feature layer

Since we want to move our trailhead locations individually, we can use
the `Select by point` tool (next to the hand) to:

1.  Select a point of interest by clicking on it.

![](images/workshop2/w2_edit-select_tool.png){fig-alt="Select by Point tool"

### Adding a New Feature

Looking around UCSB campus location, we realized that there is no point
for the campus lagoon trail!! Let's add it to the map. We will decide
that the trail starts next to the marine lab.

To add a point to our trailhead layer:

1.  Click on `New Feature` in the edit panel for this layer
2.  Your cursor should become a cross, click on the map to place your
    point
3.  Fill out the information for this new point (leave lat/long blank)
4.  Hit "Create" to add your new feature to the layer

![](images/workshop2/w2_edit-add_point.png){fig-alt="Add new feature point next to the UCSB Marine lab"
width="70%" fig-align="center"}

Make sure to get out of the `Create features` mode before clicking again
on the map!

::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
Note that the geospatial information used by ArcGIS online to display
the point is **not** store in the attribute table. This is why the
Latitude and Longitude values could be left blank and the point still
being displayed!
:::

### Editing the Attribute Table

You can also edit the information underlying the data by directly
modifying the table. You can add/remove attributes as well as directly
editing the values.

#### Adding an attribute

Now that we have added a new trailhead, we might want to add a new
attribute that will let us track if a specific point is from the
original dataset or something that we have added. You can add an
attribute using the `Field` tool on the right
![](images/workshop2/w2_field_button.png){fig-alt="Field icon that looks like text with a bar at the bottom"
width="5%"}. This should open a new panel listing all the current fields
and at the button you should see an `+ Add field` button.

1.  Click on it
2.  Choose "Numeric" -\> "Integer" & click "Next"
3.  Enter the following values & click "Add field"

![](images/workshop2/w2_field-parameters.png){fig-alt="Parameters used to create the new field"
width="90%"} Now you should have the "Added" field listed in the field
list on the right panel.

#### Editing values

Let's open the table to have a look at the values.

The new field has been added as the last column. The point we created
should be at the bottom of the table, as the last row.

There are two ways to edit values in a table. You can double-click on a
cell and change the values, or you can use the pen logo at the end of

Let's directly modify the values by double-clicking in the new "Added"

width="100%" fig-align="center"}

## Exporting Data

At some point in your analysis, you might want to also download the data
in addition to your map, for example, to move to a scripted environment
such as R and Python to conduct statistical analysis. This is a
multi-step process: first, you will have to export the feature layer in
a downloadable format; then you will be able to download this layer to
your local computer.

You can not export a layer from the Map Viewer, you will need to first
return to the “My Content” view. You can do this by using the “Burger”
menu at the top-left of your Map view and selecting Content.

-   Once in the My content view, locate and click on the spatial
    trailhead layer you imported from the CSV file to go to the Overview
    page of that layer.

![](images/workshop2/export-overview.png){fig-alt="Overview page for the feature layer of Santa Barbara County trailheads."
width="100%"}

-   Unfold the menu on the right completely, select Export data, and
    choose the GeoJSON format.

![](images/workshop2/export-overview_uncollapsed.png){fig-alt="Overview page for the feature layer of Santa Barbara County trailheads with the option menu on the right uncollapsed and showing the Export Data option"
width="100%"}

-   On the next window, leave the default options and choose your
    ucsb_bike folder as location. Click on Export. Note that exporting
    data can take some time, so be patient :)

![](images/workshop2/export-geojson.png){fig-alt="Wizard page to export a geojson file: title, Folder location, Categories, Tags and Summary are the available options"
width="50%"}

-   Once the export is completed, you should automatically be redirected
    to the Overview page of this new dataset. This time, Download should
    be available in the menu on the right side of the page. Click on it
    and select a location on your local computer and a filename.

![](images/workshop2/export-download.png){fig-alt="Overview page for the newly created geojson layer. The menu on the right has now the Download option available"
width="100%"}

### How to improve your map

#### Creating Shaded Relief (Hillshade) on the Fly

One use for a DEM is to make a shaded relief layer. That is a classic
view that gives the terrain realistic three-dimensional depth and
surface texture, we can generate a shaded relief visualization
dynamically:

1.  Duplicate the `ucsb_local_dem` layer.
2.  Rename the two DEM layers for clarity: name the top layer
    `Elevation (Color)` and the bottom layer
    `Elevation (Shaded Relief)`.
3.  Change the symbology style to **Shaded Relief**.

Shaded relief simulates how sunlight illuminates terrain, casting
shadows based on the position of the sun measured as two angles: Azimuth
and Altitude

-   **Azimuth**: The compass direction from which the illumination
    source (the sun) originates, measured in degrees clockwise from
    north (0° = North, 90° = East, 180° = South, 270° = West). In
    cartography, the sun is traditionally positioned in the northwest
    (315°) or west (270°) to match how the human brain interprets light
    and shadow, preventing an optical illusion known as "relief
    inversion" where mountains appear as valleys. For our map, we
    position the light source from the west.
-   **Altitude**: The angle of the sun above the horizon, measured from
    0° (level with the horizon at sunrise/sunset) to 90° (directly
    overhead at solar noon). A lower altitude (e.g., 30°–45°, typical of
    low winter sun) produces longer, more dramatic shadows that
    accentuate ridge lines, canyons, and valleys.

![](images/workshop2/relief_options.png)

We can adjust those angles to show the sun in the morning or evening
here in Santa Barbara.

Adjust the transparency of the top colored elevation layer so the shaded
relief beneath shows through, creating an illuminated 3D terrain effect
under our roads.

![Current status of our map with colored DEM and shaded
relief](images/workshop2/western_light.png){fig-alt="A rainbow colored hillshaded map with roads showing the software interface"}

This matches interim map 3 in our group.

This is a bit of an artificial example, because Esri offers a wide
variety of hillshade basemaps in the Living Atlas. Also: that was a
rather lengthy aside.

Now would be an excellent point to save your map.

## Preview for Workshop 3: Looking Ahead to Spatial Analysis

In Workshop 3, we dive deeper into quantitative spatial analysis. The
data layers we prepared today form the foundation for analyzing terrain
and route difficulty:

```         
- Calculate slope from the DEM (a single-channel continuous raster measuring steepness)
- Overlay slope values onto road segments
- Identify and highlight the steepest climbs (maximum slope)
```

### Analysis Workflow Overview

1.  **Slope Calculation**: Use raster analysis tools to calculate a
    slope raster from the DEM, expressing terrain steepness in degrees
    or percent rise.
2.  **Zonal Statistics as Table**: With the slope raster and the road
    network loaded, run **Raster Analysis \> Zonal Statistics as Table**
    to compute summary statistics (such as the maximum or mean slope)
    for each road line.

![](images/workshop2/create_max_slope_table.png)

3.  **Joining Statistics to Roads**: The zonal statistics tool outputs a
    standalone data table. To visualize these slope measurements on the
    map, join the table back to the road vector layer using \*\*
    Analysis \> Tools \> Summarize data \> Join Features\*\*, matching
    on a common identifier such as `OBJECTID` (which is often hidden by
    default).

**HAS ANYONE SOLVED THIS? BECAUSE THAT WOULD BE SUPER HELPFUL!!!!!**

![](images/workshop2/roads_over_slope.png)

4.  Once joined, roads can be symbolized by slope steepness, allowing us
    to pinpoint the steepest hill climbs for our ride!
